field_insights.observation: 2 paper records report Vega parallaxes of 130.23 ± 0.36 mas from the van Leeuwen (2007) Hipparcos re-reduction and 128.93 ± 0.55 mas from the original Perryman et al. (1997) Hipparcos reduction. Both are trigonometic parallaxes, and the context explicitly notes Vega is too bright for precision Gaia observations.
field_insights.interpretation: These two values are different reductions of the same Hipparcos satellite data. The difference of 1.30 mas is ~2σ when the quoted uncertainties are combined, indicating a systematic offset between the 1997 and 2007 Hipparcos reductions rather than an astrophysical change. The van Leeuwen (2007) reduction includes improved attitude reconstruction and calibration and is generally regarded as more accurate, making 130.23 mas the preferred modern value. The older 128.93 mas value is still widely used in literature and legacy catalogs. The corresponding distances are ~7.68 pc and ~7.76 pc, a ~1% difference that is negligible for many purposes but relevant for precise stellar property estimates. The lack of a Gaia parallax for Vega means Hipparcos remains the reference astrometric dataset, with a systematic uncertainty of a few tenths of a milliarcsecond.
cause_hypotheses: Systematic errors in the original 1997 Hipparcos data reduction
Improved attitude, scanning-law, and solar-wind calibration in van Leeuwen (2007)
Different reference-frame or epoch treatment between reductions
Small number of Hipparcos transits usable for a very bright, saturated source
field_insights.typical_range: Nearby bright stars: ~100–150 mas; Vega Hipparcos π ≈ 128.9–130.2 mas

field_insights.observation: 4 database records from Hipparcos, HR, and TIC give pmRA values of 201.02, 202.00000703334808, 201.02, and 201.02 mas/yr, with a range of 201.02–202.0 mas/yr. The reported methods include space astrometry, catalog compilation, and statistical cross-match inference.
field_insights.interpretation: pmRA is the right-ascension component of Vega's proper motion. The dominant value, 201.02 mas/yr, matches the Hipparcos measurement and is typical for a bright, nearby star with large apparent motion. The 202.0 mas/yr value is exactly 0.202 arcsec/yr converted to mas/yr, indicating a rounded legacy catalog value rather than a physical change in proper motion. The 0.98 mas/yr difference is only ~0.5%, but it corresponds to tens of milliarcseconds of positional drift over decades, so epoch propagation and careful cross-matching matter when combining catalogs.
cause_hypotheses: Legacy catalog value rounded to 0.202 arcsec/yr and converted to mas/yr
Different Hipparcos reductions (1997 vs 2007) yielding small systematic offsets
Catalog compilation or statistical inference in TIC reusing rounded input
field_insights.typical_range: Nearby stars: ~0–500 mas/yr; Vega pmRA ≈ 201 mas/yr

field_insights.observation: 4 database records from Hipparcos, HR, and TIC give pmDE values of 287.46, 286.00001335144043, 287.46, and 287.46 mas/yr, with a range of 286.0–287.46 mas/yr. The reported methods are the same astrometric, catalog-compilation, and cross-matching approaches as pmRA.
field_insights.interpretation: pmDE is the declination component of Vega's proper motion. The three 287.46 mas/yr entries agree with the Hipparcos value, while 286.0 mas/yr is exactly 0.286 arcsec/yr converted to mas/yr, again pointing to a rounded legacy catalog value. The ~1.46 mas/yr offset is small in relative terms (~0.5%) but not explained by any physical mechanism: proper motion is secular and linear over the timescales involved. Together with pmRA ≈ 201 mas/yr, Vega has a total proper motion of ~350 mas/yr, so any cross-catalog comparison must account for catalog epochs.
cause_hypotheses: Legacy catalog value rounded to 0.286 arcsec/yr
Different Hipparcos data reductions or catalog editions
Rounding in HR/TIC compilation rather than new astrometric measurement
Epoch or equinox mismatch among source catalogs
field_insights.typical_range: Nearby stars: ~0–500 mas/yr; Vega pmDE ≈ 287 mas/yr

cross_field_relationships.description: Parallax and RA proper motion are linked by the standard astrometric/kinematic relation: the RA component of transverse velocity is v_RA (km/s) = 4.74 * pmRA (mas/yr) / parallax (mas). For fixed transverse velocity, pmRA scales with parallax (i.e., inversely with distance). For Vega, pi ~ 130 mas and pmRA ~ 201 mas/yr imply a small RA tangential component of ~7.3 km/s. The relation is deterministic only if the transverse velocity is known; the catalog scatter between pmRA values is a systematic catalog/reduction effect, not a physical change in motion.

Parallax and Dec proper motion obey the same kinematic relation: v_Dec (km/s) = 4.74 * pmDec (mas/yr) / parallax (mas). For Vega, pi ~ 130 mas and pmDec ~ 287 mas/yr give a Dec tangential velocity component of ~10.5 km/s. The two measured fields are physically connected through the star's tangential space velocity and distance, but pmDec is not uniquely determined by parallax alone without knowledge of the velocity vector.

This pair compares the same physical quantity from different catalog reductions, not two distinct physical fields. Both values are trigonometric parallaxes of Vega from the original Hipparcos reduction (128.93 mas) and the van Leeuwen re-reduction (130.23 mas). The 1.30 mas offset reflects known systematic differences between the two reductions, not an astrophysical change or a physical relationship between separate fields.

The RA and Dec proper motion components are orthogonal components of the same total proper-motion vector. They are related by vector addition: mu_total = sqrt(pmRA^2 + pmDec^2), with position angle theta = atan2(pmDec, pmRA). For Vega, this gives mu_total ~ 350 mas/yr and a tangential motion direction defined by pmDec/pmRA ~ 1.43. There is no fixed ratio between the two components; the observed ratio reflects the direction of Vega's space velocity relative to the Sun. Both components also scale inversely with distance for a given space velocity.

suitable_use_cases: Teaching and benchmarking astrometric catalog comparisons, especially Hipparcos 1997 vs van Leeuwen 2007 reductions
Demonstrating systematic catalog offsets and rounding artifacts in bright-star astrometry
Testing database curation pipelines for duplicate detection, normalization, variance grouping, and coverage-gap reporting
Stellar kinematics exercises for bright nearby stars, using parallax and proper motion with explicit epoch and uncertainty handling
Legacy or historical studies that consistently use the original Hipparcos reduction
limitations: Overall quality score is 0.5509 with a 'fair' quality level; 3 anomalies and 3 variance groups indicate inconsistent or heterogeneous inputs
Vega has no Gaia precision parallax because it is too bright, so Hipparcos remains the reference astrometric dataset and carries known systematic offsets between reductions
The two HIPPARCOS parallax values differ by ~1.3 mas: 130.23 ± 0.36 mas (van Leeuwen 2007) vs 128.93 ± 0.55 mas (Perryman et al. 1997), producing a ~1% distance ambiguity
Proper-motion fields contain rounded legacy conversions: pmRA = 202.0 mas/yr and pmDE = 286.0 mas/yr are exactly 0.202 and 0.286 arcsec/yr converted to mas/yr, not independent modern measurements
Coverage gaps exist: references 2020AN....341..860R and 2006ApJ...645..664A are missing pmra and pmdec, limiting their use for full astrometric solutions
This is a small, single-object dataset; it is not representative of a wide-area catalog and is unsuitable for population-level statistical studies
recommended_caveats: Use the van Leeuwen (2007) Hipparcos parallax 130.23 ± 0.36 mas as the preferred modern value; if using 128.93 ± 0.55 mas, explicitly state that it is the original 1997 reduction
Do not average parallax or proper-motion values across different reductions or catalogs; choose one consistent source and propagate its uncertainties
Treat pmRA = 201.02 mas/yr and pmDE = 287.46 mas/yr as the consistent modern values; treat 202.0 and 286.0 mas/yr as rounded legacy representations, not independent measurements
Account for catalog epochs and equinoxes when propagating proper motions; even a ~0.5% proper-motion offset can produce tens of milliarcseconds of positional drift over decades
For distance-sensitive stellar properties, include the systematic Hipparcos uncertainty and the ~1% distance difference between 7.68 pc and 7.76 pc

When computing transverse velocity, use consistent units: v_tan(km/s) = 4.74 * mu(mas/yr) / parallax(mas); for Vega this yields about 7.3 km/s in RA and 10.5 km/s in Dec, but these are illustrative only

If filling coverage gaps for pmra/pmdec, obtain both values from the same high-quality epoch-aware source, e.g., the van Leeuwen (2007) Hipparcos catalog, rather than inferring from rounded legacy values
When combining TIC/HR/Hipparcos records, track source versions and compilation provenance closely; apparent scatter may reflect rounding or reduction choices rather than real astrophysical variation

overall_narrative: The assessment covers four astrometric fields and four cross-field relationships for Vega, with an overall grade of fair. The dominant proper-motion components—pmRA of 201.02 mas/yr and pmDE values near 287.46 mas/yr—are consistent with Hipparcos and typical of a bright, nearby star with large apparent motion. However, different reductions of the same Hipparcos data show a 1.30 mas parallax offset at roughly 2σ significance, pointing to a systematic rather than random discrepancy. One declination entry (286.0 mas/yr) appears to be a simple unit-conversion artifact from 0.286 arcsec/yr, indicating heterogeneous data sources. Overall, the dataset broadly matches established astrometry for Vega but contains subtle systematic offsets and conversion inconsistencies that merit caution.
